implement: legion-worker: the implementer's own charter — the pull request body and its proof rules, the one push procedure, the review-thread and merge-gate references, and the rule that a finding outside this issue is a dispatch ask and never a new issue.

dispatch-first: the open human to-do (dispatch://INFRA-271/ask/b51ee5d5-d1bc-4d85-974e-c0f135a8c122) and any further Dispatch write must be searched for first; this plan's own prior art (dispatch://INFRA-244) was found that way.
dispatch: every write this phase makes to Dispatch — a reply under the open ask, a message when the live proof lands — follows its rules for writing to a person who has not read the code.

ce-simplify-code: the implementer's simplify pass over the settled change before the phase completes, which this change needs because it touches one parser, one manifest builder and one long-lived process.
test: legion-worker: the tester drives the application rather than re-running the suite, reads lint, types and unit suites from CI, and records its proof as a command, an observation, a head SHA and a negative control.
dispatch-first: before posting any finding, to reach the issue that already tracks it rather than opening a second record.
dispatch: for the finding itself, which is a dispatch ask on the issue it belongs to.
review: legion-worker: the review round's order and its review-thread and merge-gate references, which govern how each thread is answered and resolved and what READY may carry.
ce-simplify-code: the standard the reviewer holds the simplify pass to, since this change adds a package and a third configuration mode and is where needless abstraction would land.

findings.finding: Acceptance criterion 3 asks that two pods of different issues show different database logins, but every pod is built with the one service account the configuration names (internal/runtime/sandbox/manifest.go:414-415), so every pod presents one identity and one database login.
findings.answer: Measured and escalated to the tree's architect, which took it to the person; the root spec's acceptance line at version 15 now reads that pods share the one login their platform identity maps to, and the plan is written against that line (plan.md section 6 and departure 1).

findings.finding: The spec never says where the agent's new connection file lives, and the two obvious places are unusable: the providers Secret is mounted read-only (manifest.go:614-616) and the launcher empties its private directory at every generation start (launcher.go:384-392).
findings.answer: Decision D3: the launcher writes the connection string into the generation's own directory beside the boot token, and the daemon points OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE at it through shimwire.LauncherStart.Env, exactly as it points LEGION_BOOT_TOKEN_FILE (runtime/sandbox/launcher.go:414). The URL's content never changes; the file belongs to one generation, as one agent process does.

findings.finding: The launcher's own resume lookup runs before writeFiles (launcher.go:264-270 ahead of :272), so a credential whose lifetime starts beside writeFiles cannot serve the second database client the issue scopes.
findings.answer: Decision D4 and task 4: writeFiles moves ahead of resumable, the connection file and the proxy are created between them, and the generation directory is removed on a refused resume as the failed-start path already does (:286).

findings.finding: Six role containers share one network namespace, so a loopback proxy needs a port rule and an answer to who may dial it.
findings.answer: Decision D2: a port per role, a fixed base plus the role's index in names.go, bound to 127.0.0.1 and never 0.0.0.0. Any process in the issue's pod can dial it, which is the trade the shared URL file already makes (docs/kubernetes.md:545-549); this change removes the password, not that trade. The plan's risk list has the implementer check the pod's listening sockets before fixing the base.

findings.finding: The spec requires that a credential expiring at the wrong moment be impossible rather than unlikely, but gives the proxy no behaviour for a credential it cannot obtain or refresh.
findings.answer: Decision D5: the proxy proves one upstream connection at generation start and refuses the launch with a named error when it cannot, so no agent runs without a working credential path; an accepted connection whose upstream dial fails is closed at once and never answered; each failure is one line on the role container's log. Task 3 tests all three.

findings.finding: Criterion 2 names no observable, and the behaviour it probes may never occur: the agent's pool closes a connection five seconds after the last write, so a fresh credential per connection satisfies it without any refresh.
findings.answer: Split in plan.md section 6: the mechanism is proven by a sessionproxy test where a second connection after the first credential's expiry mints a second credential, and the live half is the production check after the merge, comparing an INFRA pod's start time with its conversation row's mtime_ms.

findings.finding: Criterion 1 is already true today, because the deployment runs session_store: pvc and no worker pod holds a session URL, so it decides nothing.
findings.answer: Recorded as departure 4 and in plan.md section 2: the password store arrives with dispatch://INFRA-244, which is in testing, so the password exists from that merge onward. Section 6 restates the criterion as checks that can fail: no session key in the providers Secret, no such file in the pod's mount, a URL with no user-info password, and the daemon's own refusal of session_dsn_secret under the new store.

findings.finding: All four criteria describe a live Cloud SQL instance only a person can put into that state: the instance flag, the identity and the grant are deployment-repository work, and sqladmin answers the pod 403 today.
findings.answer: dispatch://INFRA-271/ask/b51ee5d5-d1bc-4d85-974e-c0f135a8c122 is open with that to-do and its options. plan.md section 8 names what waits for it (three rows of the acceptance table) and what does not (tasks 1 to 7 and every test), so the phase proceeds while the person answers.

findings.finding: The proof the parent plan names cannot exercise the design: stage 4a's session-store step starts a throwaway Postgres in Docker with a password, which has no metadata server and no Cloud SQL connector.
findings.answer: Task 8 adds a check of its own, session-identity, run when the operator supplies the instance, the database, the login and a URL file their own machine can reach, and skipped with a printed reason otherwise, as the bridge check already is (stage4a-sandbox-runtime.sh:328-334). postgres-resume stays unchanged, because the password store stays.

findings.finding: The grant must let the login create Oh My Pi's two tables, not only log in: since Postgres 15, CREATE on the database is not enough and the create is refused with permission denied for schema public (docs/kubernetes.md:535-540).
findings.answer: plan.md section 8 names it as part of what the person's answer settles, and task 7 carries it into the documentation of the new store; the ask asks for a database user that can sign in to the database that holds the conversations, which is the database whose schema the login must be able to create in.

findings.finding: How the proxy authenticates is left open, and the three candidate mechanisms imply very different work.
findings.answer: Decision D1 chooses automatic IAM database authentication through the Cloud SQL Go connector, which submits the token for the password attribute so the proxy never parses the Postgres wire protocol; the alternative would add several hundred lines of protocol for no gain. Its costs are named: one direct dependency and the Cloud SQL client role beside the sign-in role.

findings.finding: movedSessionStore keys on the projected Secret item (addresses.go:281-307), so under a store whose URL is not a Secret key held and handed are both empty and a pod created under the old store is never replaced.
findings.answer: Task 5: movedSessionStore compares the store a running pod carries with the one a pod launched now would get — the Secret key under postgres, the four launcher flags under the new store, and a change of kind either way — so the replacement guarantee survives.

findings.finding: The configuration surface has eight consumers besides the manifest, and the issue mentions none of them.
findings.answer: Tasks 1, 2, 6 and 7 name each: the parser and its refusals, the runtime options, providers(), mainEnvironment, sessionsInDatabase, the launcher container's flags, the operator-pod reserved-name refusals, the reported settings and their three fixtures, the image probe's marker rule and its pod, and the documentation sections and runbooks.

findings.finding: The second database client undercounts: legion sessions import and legion sessions mark-lost also open the same database with a --dsn-file URL, from a machine with no launcher and no proxy.
findings.answer: Decision D7: both commands are unchanged and keep their flag; the documentation task says the operator supplies a URL their own machine can reach. Nothing in this change removes that path.

findings.finding: Four of the spec's load-bearing statements are not verifiable from this repository; the strict open is corroborated, the read-once and pool claims are not, and the opening sentence is false of the deployment as it runs today.
findings.answer: The strict open is cited where the plan relies on it (docs/kubernetes.md:478-483, D5). The read-once and pool claims are the architect's own reading of the deployed binary, recorded under Child H of the parent plan, and nothing in this plan depends on the pool numbers. The opening sentence is departure 4.

findings.finding: Two smaller traps: this repository is public and its check fails on text naming the deployment, and the word listener already names the worker stream's listener in the files this work touches.
findings.answer: plan.md's risk list states the public-name rule and what it covers; the in-pod component is named the session database proxy throughout, and the new package is internal/sessionproxy, so no file calls it a listener.

specDepartures.spec: The issue's own acceptance list reads: two pods of different issues show different database logins in the database's own view of its connections, and the shared login has none.
specDepartures.plan: The plan proves instead that no pod holds a password, that every connection carries a credential minted inside that pod from its own identity and never written to disk, and that the password login has no connections left and its password is nowhere; pods share the one login their platform identity maps to. The tree's architect took the measurement to the person and the root spec's acceptance line at version 15 now reads that way, so the plan follows the root spec.
specDepartures.evidence: internal/runtime/sandbox/manifest.go:414-415 builds every pod with the one service account the configuration names; measured in a live INFRA worker pod on 2026-10-25, the pod's cloud identity is the cluster's workload identity pool and sqladmin answers its token HTTP 403. Per-issue logins would mean Legion creating cloud identities and database users as it launches.

acceptance: Two pods of different issues show different database logins in the database's own view of its connections, and the shared login has none.

specDepartures.spec: The design the spec incorporates by reference (dispatch://INFRA-228/artifact/plan-md, Child H) says the credential is obtained before the worker starts, beside writeFiles.
specDepartures.plan: The credential and the proxy are created before the resume lookup, and writeFiles moves ahead of it, with the generation directory removed on a refused resume.
specDepartures.evidence: packages/daemon/internal/launcher/launcher.go:264-270 runs resumable before writeFiles at :272, and resumable is the second database client the issue scopes; the failed-start path at :286 already removes the directory.

specDepartures.spec: The parent plan's departure note says the instance flag that turns on the database's identity login needs no restart, and asks for no window.
specDepartures.plan: The plan treats the restart as unsettled and as the person's check before the apply, in the open ask's options.
specDepartures.evidence: Google's own flag documentation and a public report both say enabling cloudsql.iam_authentication restarts the instance. The tree's architect confirmed on 2026-10-25 that the conversation database is moving to an instance of its own, so the restart's cost is bounded to the conversations rather than to Dispatch, the secrets broker and every Legion daemon.

specDepartures.spec: The spec opens by saying the whole connection URL, password and all, is one key of that project's secret, mounted into every pod.
specDepartures.plan: The plan records that as what the configuration can express rather than what the deployment runs, and names dispatch://INFRA-244 as the issue turning it on.
specDepartures.evidence: No stack in the deployment repository sets session_store at all, read on 2026-10-25; dispatch://INFRA-244, which creates the password database and sets the two keys, was in testing when this plan was written.
